title: Sharks: Ancient and Endangered
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Sharks have lived in the oceans for more than four hundred million years, which is longer than trees have existed on land and about two hundred million years before the first dinosaurs. There are over five hundred species, ranging from the dwarf lanternshark, which would fit in a human hand, to the whale shark, which can reach twelve metres in length. In films, sharks are shown as man-eating monsters, but in reality they are mostly shy animals, and fewer than a dozen people die from shark attacks in a typical year. In contrast, humans kill tens of millions of sharks annually. This passage describes how sharks live and why they need our protection.

Sharks differ from most fish in having a skeleton made of cartilage, the flexible material of which our ears and noses are made, rather than bone. Cartilage is lighter than bone, which helps a shark to float. Its skin is covered with tiny tooth-like scales, called denticles, which make it rough to the touch, like sandpaper, and which reduce drag as the shark swims. Sharks also have no swim bladder, the gas-filled organ that many fish use to stay at a given depth; instead, they have a large oil-filled liver, and many species must keep swimming to avoid sinking.

Shark teeth are remarkable. Sharks do not have a single set of teeth but rows of them, which are constantly replaced. When a tooth is lost, one from the row behind moves forward, like a conveyor belt. Some sharks may grow and lose tens of thousands of teeth in a lifetime. The shape of the teeth shows how the shark feeds: sharp, narrow teeth for gripping slippery fish, broad, serrated teeth for cutting large prey, and flat teeth for crushing shellfish. The whale shark and the basking shark, the two largest, have tiny teeth and instead filter plankton from the water.

Sharks have an extraordinary set of senses. Their sense of smell is acute: some species can detect a drop of blood diluted in a swimming pool of water. They also have good vision in dim light. In addition, they have a unique sense organ, called the ampullae of Lorenzini, a network of tiny jelly-filled pores around the snout which can detect the weak electrical fields produced by the muscles of other animals. A shark can find a fish hidden in sand by its electricity alone. Along the sides of the body, a line of sensitive cells detects vibrations in the water, so that a shark can feel an injured fish from far away.

Reproduction in sharks is varied and slow. Some species lay eggs in tough cases, often called mermaid's purses, which are attached to seaweed or rocks. Others keep the eggs inside the body until they hatch and give birth to live young, and in some species, the embryo is nourished through a link like a placenta, as in mammals. Sharks grow slowly and mature late: some species do not breed until they are twenty or even thirty years old. They produce few young, and the great white shark may live for seventy years. Because of this, a shark population cannot recover quickly if too many are killed.

Today, sharks are in danger. An estimated one hundred million sharks are killed every year, mostly in fishing nets and on long lines, many as an unwanted by-catch. Others are caught for their fins, which are used in a soup in some countries; often the fins are cut off and the body is thrown back into the sea. About a third of shark and ray species are now considered threatened with extinction. Dr Jonas Eriksen, a marine biologist who studies sharks with underwater cameras, points out that this has consequences beyond the sharks themselves, because many are top predators that keep the numbers of other species in balance.

There are signs of hope. Many countries now ban the finning of sharks, and some have created sanctuaries where fishing for sharks is forbidden. In some places, divers who pay to see sharks bring more money to the local economy than fishermen who kill them. Dr Eriksen urges consumers to avoid shark products and to choose fish from sustainable sources. He also hopes that attitudes are changing. Young people, he says, are growing up with a different picture of sharks, not as monsters but as ancient and important animals, which have survived several mass extinctions and deserve a place in the future.
